children: European wheat edged up on Thursday, steadying after a one-week low as traders assessed latest attacks in Russia's war with Ukraine, while looking to U.S. government grain forecasts on Friday for further direction.
December wheat
on Euronext was 0.1% up at €245 ($284.89) a metric ton at 1539 GMT.
The benchmark contract earlier touched a one-week low at €243.25, moving further from last week's contract high of €259.25, before regaining ground.
Chicago wheat
was up about 1%, rebounding from an earlier two-week low.

Renewed diplomatic moves to end Russia's war with Ukraine have weighed on prices, though more Russian attacks on Thursday, including one on the Ukrainian city of Dnipro that damaged a vegetable oil factory of U.S. agrifood group Bunge
, kept attention on continuing disruption to the massive Black Sea grain trade.
The run-up to the U.S. Department of Agriculture's supply and demand forecasts on Friday encouraged profit-taking by investors who have built up a large long position in wheat.
"Wheat is likely to remain highly headline-driven into Friday's USDA report," British merchant ADM Agriculture said.
"The market needs to reconcile severe Black Sea execution risk with limited evidence of stronger U.S. or EU demand and extreme fund length," it said in a note.
The USDA report is being closely watched as a gauge of U.S. corn and soybean yields, as well as the effects of Black Sea disruption on global grain trade.
"Russian and Ukrainian ship-borne Black Sea exports are tiny compared to normal volumes," a German trader said.
"But low Black Sea prices continue to encourage some importers to delay buying in case some deal could enable Russian and Ukrainian grain ships to sail again.”

Russian Black Sea prices were hard to assess but theoretically $80-$90 a ton below west European levels on a free-on-board basis, the trader said, adding Russian wheat from the Baltic Sea was quoted about $10-$20 below western Europe.
Russian 11.5% Black Sea wheat was nominally around $203-$208 a ton for September/October shipment while Russian Baltic Sea wheat was at around $272-$276 a ton, the trader said.
Commodity data firm Expana raised its outlook for European Union soft wheat exports this season as reduced Black Sea shipments shifted demand to the bloc.
